newsitem.title: USA: Clinton seeks fast track trade negotiating power.
newsitem.headline: Clinton seeks fast track trade negotiating power.

text.p: President Clinton urged Congress on Tuesday to give him authority to negotiate new trade pacts, saying that the United States needed to expand its exports to Asia and Latin America.

In remarks prepared for delivery in his State of the Union address to Congress and the nation, Clinton also vowed to pursue closer ties with China and said he planned to visit Beijing to help bring that about.

"We have worked hard to tear down trade barriers abroad, so that we can create good jobs at home," Clinton said. "America is once again the most competitive nation, and the number one exporter in the world."
But he made clear that the United States could not rest on its laurels.

"We must act to expand our exports, especially to Asia and Latin America, the two fastest growing regions on earth, or be left behind as these emerging economies forge new ties with other nations," Clinton said.
"That is why we need the authority now to conclude new trade agreements that open markets to our goods and services even as we preserve our values," he added.
The administration is seeking "fast track" negotiating authority that would prevent lawmakers from holding up trade agreements or subjecting them to endless amendments.

While many Republican lawmakers are sympathetic to U.S. efforts to expand trade, they are reluctant to grant Clinton such a wide authority because the Democratic president also wants the power to negotiate labor and environmental standards.

If Congress grants Clinton "fast track" powers, that would allow the administration to restart negotiations with Chile on its entry into the North American Free Trade Agreement with Canada and Mexico.

Clinton hailed the success of his controversial economic rescue package for Mexico, noting that the Latin American nation has repaid all the money it borrowed from Washington and that U.S. exports to its southern neighbor are at an all-time high.

The president said the United States also "must pursue a deeper dialogue with China" because working with China, instead of isolating it, is the best way to work out differences. "An isolated China is not good for America," he said. "A China playing its proper role in the world is."
Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin have pledged to make reciprocal visits.

"I will go to China and I have invited China's president to come here, not because we agree on everything, but because engaging China is the best way to work on common challenges like ending nuclear testing -- and to deal frankly with fundamental differences like human rights," Clinton said.
